asset_policy: dsl_primary_with_supporting_assets; no supporting assets used - every frame is pure DSL and no Image element appears anywhere in the portfolio
curatorial_statement: Ten everyday information problems, each solved as its own artefact with its own visual language: a fridge-door medicine chart, a clinical track chart, a bill waterfall, a pay flow, an insurance verdict grid, a portion poster, a connection time budget, a fare cost surface, a bin-store poster and a laundry cost comparison. The link between them is method, not styling: each one replaces a document organised by the system that produced it with one organised by the decision the reader has to make.

fictional: all brands, products, patients, households, councils and insurers
all prices, tariffs, meter readings and salaries
the station, the platforms and the connection timings
standard_published_values: income tax bands, NI rate and student loan threshold
WHO free-sugar guidance, salt and fibre reference values
typical washing machine energy and water consumption
not_verified: no user testing, field measurement or expert review was performed
portion sizes, walking times and appliance figures are typical values, not measurements taken for this portfolio

cases.title: Five medicines, one day
cases.audience: A 68-year-old taking five medicines, and the adult daughter who does the repeats
cases.use_context: Printed at A3 and stuck on the fridge door; also read on a phone at the pharmacy
cases.user_goal: Run the day without a timing clash, and know what to do about a missed dose
cases.content_basis: Five prescriptions, seven doses a day, and rules that only exist on the boxes: levothyroxine needs an empty stomach and four hours from iron and calcium, iron and calcium need two hours between them, and two of the doses clash.
cases.visual_intent: A 24-hour band with every dose on a spoke, the clashes bracketed in red, and a table that turns each box's small print into one line
cases.dsl_capabilities: Time axis from minutes, lane assignment so no two dose labels collide, red clash bars with numbered badges, zebra table, printed-paper palette
cases.completion_criteria: Every dose is visible with its time; both clashes are named with the gap and the requirement; the fixed schedule is on the same sheet

cases.title: Your blood results, in range
cases.audience: The same patient, the evening the results arrive, before the GP appointment
cases.use_context: Desktop or tablet at home, then printed and taken to the appointment
cases.user_goal: Know which results need a conversation, and which way each one is moving
cases.content_basis: A printout of twelve numbers with a reference range in brackets. Nobody can tell which ones matter, which way they moved, or by how much.
cases.visual_intent: Reference ranges as horizontal tracks: the band is the range, a hollow marker is the last result, a filled marker is now, so direction of travel is visible without numbers
cases.dsl_capabilities: Per-row adaptive scale so every marker fits, range bands, hollow/filled markers, out-of-range rows promoted to full cards with plain-language meanings
cases.completion_criteria: The six out-of-range results are separated from the six normal ones; each row shows value, unit, range and change; nothing is clipped
cases.visual_review: Viewed case-02 v1 (B06-REQ-0002), v2 (0004) and final (0028)

cases.title: Why this bill is £34.66 higher
cases.audience: A two-adult household on a variable tariff
cases.use_context: Desktop, the evening the bill lands, with the previous bill to hand
cases.user_goal: See how much of the increase is weather, how much is price, and what would actually reduce it
cases.content_basis: An electricity bill that jumped a third in a month, with no explanation beyond a kWh figure and a colder October.
cases.visual_intent: A waterfall from last month's bill to this month's, with degree days named as the cause and a ranked list of what would bring it down
cases.dsl_capabilities: Floating waterfall bars with dashed connectors, wrapped labels under each bar, month-comparison rail, ranked saving bars
cases.completion_criteria: The four reasons sum exactly to the bill difference; the weather share is named as weather; the actions are ranked by pounds

cases.title: Your pay, and where it goes
cases.audience: Anyone on PAYE who has never checked what the deductions buy
cases.use_context: Desktop at home, once a year, usually in January
cases.user_goal: See the split between take-home, tax, NI, pension and loan, and what each buys
cases.content_basis: A payslip lists deductions in an order that hides the proportions: the biggest number on the page is not the one that reaches the bank.
cases.visual_intent: A flow: one gross bar splitting into five destination bars through translucent ribbons, with the percentage inside each destination
cases.dsl_capabilities: Scanline-filled quadrilaterals for the ribbons, proportional widths, band arithmetic (allowance, basic rate, NI threshold, loan threshold) computed in the data model
cases.completion_criteria: The five parts sum to gross; the take-home share is stated; each deduction has a plain-language line

cases.title: What your policy does not cover
cases.audience: A householder deciding whether to claim, or whether to add accidental damage
cases.use_context: Desktop, after something has gone wrong, in a hurry
cases.user_goal: Find the verdict for a specific situation in seconds, and see the six refusals that cause most disputes
cases.content_basis: Home insurance is sold on what it covers and claimed against on what it excludes; the exclusions are spread through 40 pages.
cases.visual_intent: Eighteen real situations sorted by verdict, colour-coded, each with the reason in one line, and the six common refusals called out
cases.dsl_capabilities: Sorted tile grid, verdict chips, per-tile accent bars, wrapping reason lines
cases.completion_criteria: Covered, conditional and excluded are visually distinct and sorted so the good news and the bad news are separate; every tile has a reason

cases.title: One bowl, most of your day's sugar
cases.audience: A parent buying granola, reading the label in the shop or the kitchen
cases.use_context: A3 or A4 poster in the kitchen; also readable on a phone at the shelf
cases.user_goal: See what one real bowl costs against a whole day's sugar, fat, salt and fibre
cases.content_basis: A cereal box calls 45 g a serving and prints percentages against it. A real bowl is 80 g, and the sugar goes from a third of a day to two thirds.
cases.visual_intent: Two bowls drawn to the portion, not a table: the label bowl is nearly empty and the real bowl is nearly full, then four day-budget bars with the label notch
cases.dsl_capabilities: Semicircle scanline fill for the bowls, fill level driven by grams, budget bars with a label marker, computed reference-value shares
cases.completion_criteria: The two portions are visually different at a glance; the 45 g fiction is named; fibre is shown as the good news

cases.title: You have eight minutes
cases.audience: A traveller with one bag, changing trains at a big station
cases.use_context: Phone on the platform, between the doors opening and the next departure
cases.user_goal: Know whether the connection is comfortable, tight or already lost, and what happens if the first train is late
cases.content_basis: A tight connection is decided by walking distances, stairs and a ticket-gate queue, none of which appear on the ticket.
cases.visual_intent: A time budget built from eight real legs against an eight-minute axis, with the slack shown as a block and the delay scenarios below
cases.dsl_capabilities: Minute-scaled Gantt bars, per-leg colour by kind of movement, slack block, red departure line, delay scenario cards
cases.completion_criteria: Every leg is named and timed, the total equals the available time, and the delay scenarios say makes it or miss it explicitly

cases.title: Which ticket is cheapest for the way you travel
cases.audience: A commuter deciding between paying as they go and buying a pass
cases.use_context: Desktop, at the kitchen table, once a year (or after a fare rise)
cases.user_goal: Find the cheapest option for a stated number of journeys a week and weeks a year
cases.content_basis: Five ticket types, four caps and a pass, and no way to tell which one is cheaper for a pattern that is not the one in the advert.
cases.visual_intent: A cost surface rather than a price list: journeys a week down, weeks a year across, and the cheapest option printed in every cell
cases.dsl_capabilities: Computed five-option comparison per cell, colour-coded winners, highlighted user pattern, notes that explain why the weekly cap almost never wins
cases.completion_criteria: Every cell names its cheapest option and cost; the user's own pattern is highlighted; the dominated options are explained rather than hidden

cases.title: Which bin does this go in?
cases.audience: Residents at the bin store, and anyone doing a clear-out
cases.use_context: A3 poster screwed to the bin-store wall, read standing up with a bag in one hand
cases.user_goal: Decide the bin for nine awkward items, and know the one rule that covers most of the rest
cases.content_basis: Kerbside rules are published as a list of materials, but the decisions people actually face are objects: a greasy pizza box, a broken glass, a kettle.
cases.visual_intent: Object-first cards with the verdict as a coloured chip, the reason underneath, and a small contamination panel
cases.dsl_capabilities: Object cards with verdict chips, kerbside summary table, rule-of-thumb panel, contaminant list
cases.completion_criteria: Nine real items each end in one named destination with a reason; the 'smaller than a fist' rule is stated; contaminants are named

cases.title: What a wash really costs
cases.audience: A household running four washes a week
cases.use_context: Desktop or tablet, read once when the machine is next to be replaced
cases.user_goal: Pick the programme that is cheap enough without leaving clothes unhygienic
cases.content_basis: Washing machine programmes are labelled by temperature and time, not by cost, and the difference between 30 and 60 is nearly half the running cost.
cases.visual_intent: Six programme cards with cost per wash and per year, a sorted cost chart, and a note on what each temperature actually removes
cases.dsl_capabilities: Cost model from energy, water and detergent, per-programme stacked mini-bars, sorted comparison bars, dark instrument palette
cases.completion_criteria: Cost per wash and per year are on every card; the saving between 30 and 60 is stated in pounds; hygiene limits are stated too

final_collection_review: All ten finals were opened at 100 % after the per-piece passes. The set deliberately has no shared grid, palette or type scale: the sizes run from 900x1440 to 1600x1130, four pieces are dark and six are light, and the visual metaphors (band, track, waterfall, ribbon, verdict tile, bowl, Gantt, matrix, object card, cost chart) are chosen per problem. What they share is the discipline that every number comes from tools/b06_data.py, that the arithmetic on the image balances, and that nothing is a placeholder. Two pieces needed a second look after the first render was accepted (case-03's rail note, case-05's two wrapping titles); both were fixed and re-rendered rather than shipped.
unresolved_issues: case-08's smallest cells are dense; a print version would need a larger sheet.
No user testing was performed, so all readability claims are design judgements.
Three documents were rejected by the service for the same class of syntax error (a border without width and style); all three are recorded as real failures in requests.jsonl.
